title: Beyond Cognitive Load Theory
author: Peter Ellerton
summary: Ellerton argues that Cognitive Load Theory (CLT), positioned in K-12 discourse as the Science of Learning, has been stretched far beyond its evidential and conceptual limits. CLT began as a narrow theory of instructional efficiency for novices acquiring tightly structured knowledge, not a comprehensive philosophy of education, and treating it as one is a category error. Drawing on a recent Brain Sciences paper, Ellerton brings in cognitive reserve and brain reserve from neuroscience to argue that working memory emerges from dynamic neural networks shaped by emotion, motivation, fatigue, and prior experience, making over-minimised classrooms developmentally counterproductive. He flags what CLT leaves out, emotion, sociality, and self-regulation, which neuroscience treats as constitutive rather than peripheral to learning. The piece pushes back on the rigid intrinsic/extraneous/germane load distinction, noting that the brain's default mode network requires the very mind-wandering and conflict CLT pedagogy aggressively suppresses. The closing alternative reframes load as something to be adaptively managed rather than uniformly minimised, with challenge as a resource and education aimed at cultivating agency rather than optimising instruction for the next test.
points: CLT's K-12 promotion as a comprehensive theory of learning is a category error; it began as a narrow theory of instructional efficiency for novices acquiring tightly structured knowledge.
Cognitive reserve and brain reserve from neuroscience show that learning capacity grows through challenge, novelty, and emotional engagement, not through the aggressive minimisation of difficulty.
CLT systematically sidelines emotion, social interaction, and self-regulation; neuroscience treats these as constitutive of learning, not peripheral.

The intrinsic/extraneous/germane load distinction has limited neural support; moderate distraction and mind-wandering activate the default mode network, which is crucial for creativity and consolidation.
The healthier reframe is productive friction (not zero friction) and adaptively managed load, with education aimed at capacity tomorrow rather than efficiency today.
quotes: CLT began life as a theory about instructional efficiency under constrained conditions, especially for novice learners acquiring tightly structured knowledge. It was never intended as a theory of human development, nor as a comprehensive philosophy of education.

Working memory emerges from dynamic neural networks that adapt to task demands, emotional salience, motivation, fatigue, and prior experience. Instruction designed solely to reduce load may feel supportive in the short term, but it risks under-challenging the very systems that need to develop.
Children are not fragile information processors waiting to be protected from difficulty. They are unusually exploratory, socially attuned, and cognitively plastic.

Neuroscience consistently shows that emotion and cognition are deeply intertwined. Emotional context influences attention and memory consolidation; motivation alters cognitive capacity; social interaction reshapes neural networks.

If learners are never asked to manage complexity themselves, they never learn how. The result is a troubling irony: an approach intended to make learning easier may produce students less capable of learning independently.

Even more counterintuitive is the evidence around so-called 'extraneous' load. Moderate distraction, cognitive conflict, and even periods of apparent mind-wandering activate the brain's default mode network, something that is crucial for creativity, insight, and consolidation.
If CLT helped correct an era of unguided discovery, it should not now become the justification for an era of over-managed learning.” Archived from Peter Ellerton Substack on May 1, 2026 by Tim.
